nutshell: Metro Detroit is a heritage-music giant with a thin Anglo-Celtic trad scene. Inside the six-county MSA the verified participatory calendar is only about 50 events a month: one weekly Irish pub session (in Plymouth), one monthly contra (in Troy), a few bluegrass jams, and, surprisingly, twice-weekly international folk dance as the busiest trad activity. Ann Arbor, a separate 370,000-person MSA 40 miles west, runs about as many trad events as all of metro Detroit and hosts The Ark, the region's real folk club. Yet Detroit's folk history is among America's richest: French habitant fiddling, Henry Ford's 1920s dance crusade, Lomax's 1938 recordings of Serbian gusle and Delta blues, a Cape Breton fiddling hub, the Hillbilly Highway, Joni Mitchell's coffeehouse years. Its living traditions are Arab and Chaldean music in Dearborn, about 550 Polish folk-dance students, tamburica and bandura orchestras, Black gospel quartets, blues jams, and a new Detroit Folk School reviving square dance.

organizations.name: Detroit United Quartet Ministries
organizations.notes: Co-presenter of the Motown Museum quartet showcases.

organizations.name: GMWA Detroit Chapter / GMWA Detroit Mass Choir
organizations.kind: gospel workshop chapter and community choir
organizations.notes: GMWA founded by Rev. James Cleveland in 1967 in Detroit; first board meeting in Detroit March 1968 and first national convention at King Solomon Church that summer. The chapter has had nine local leaders and held twelve national posts. Mass choir recordings: Detroit Remembers Vol. 1 (2001), Vol. 2 (2006), Tribute to the King. Sister-choir exchange with Chicago's GMAC every two years since 2011. Led by Iris A. Taylor, Ph.D.; open to all.

organizations.name: GMWA Quartet Division (Detroit)
organizations.notes: Chairman: Bishop Kenneth Robinson Sr. Small online presence (~40 likes).

organizations.name: Detroit Gospel Music Legacy Foundation
organizations.notes: 501(c)(3) documenting Detroit gospel artists and church music.

organizations.name: DetroitGospel.com
organizations.notes: Calendar of church anniversaries, tributes (e.g. 'Detroit Remembers Richard Smallwood', Oct 9-10 2026) and free concerts; ~2,700 Facebook followers.

organizations.name: Fasola Michigan
organizations.notes: Lists Lansing, Kalamazoo (2), Ann Arbor, Ypsilanti and Grand Rapids. No Detroit-MSA group is listed.

organizations.name: Earthwork Music
organizations.notes: Founded by Seth Bernard on his family farm in Lake City; statewide. Detroit songwriter Jo Serrapere is an Earthwork artist.

organizations.name: Windsor Folk Music and Arts Society
organizations.notes: Windsor, ON; concerts and open mics at Mackenzie Hall. No 2024-26 evidence found, status unverified.

organizations.name: Arab American National Museum (ACCESS)
organizations.notes: Opened May 5 2005 in Dearborn; Smithsonian affiliate; 156-seat Aliya Hassan Auditorium; produces the Concert of Colors Forum; hosts dabke classes and oud/tabla/riqq lessons.

organizations.name: National Arab Orchestra (NAO) / NAO Takht Ensemble / NAO Community Choir
organizations.notes: Founded by Michael Ibrahim; first concert April 4 2009 at U-M Moore Organ Recital Hall, Ann Arbor (originally Michigan Arab Orchestra; takht established April 2010). Building Bridges Through Music: free after-school Arab music program for Detroit public school students. Nov 8 2026 concert 'The Songs We Carry'.

organizations.name: Chaldean Cultural Center
organizations.notes: Inside Shenandoah Country Club, West Bloomfield; billed as the world's first and only Chaldean museum (ClickOnDetroit 2019). Chaldean Community Foundation opened a 42,000 sq ft CCF West building in 2025.

organizations.name: Ukrainian American Archives & Museum of Detroit
organizations.notes: Founded by Roman and Ivanka Dacko; now in Hamtramck (9630 Joseph Campau); 20,000-book library; musical instruments; UBC performs there.

organizations.name: Ukrainian Cultural Center
organizations.notes: 26601 Ryan Rd, Warren; 'heart of the Ukrainian community in Southeastern Michigan'.

organizations.name: Ukrainian Bandurist Chorus of North America
organizations.notes: Kyiv 1918 (uninterrupted lineage from 1941); whole ensemble (17 families) immigrated 1949, sponsored by Sol Hurok and Detroit lawyer John Panchuk, settling in Hamtramck. ~50 men aged 16-70; some third-generation bandurists; NEA Heritage Fellowship 2025, Michigan Heritage Award 2022. | Founded in Kyiv in 1918; in metro Detroit since 1949.

organizations.name: 'Zora' Lodge 351, Croatian Fraternal Union (American Croatian Club)
organizations.notes: Warren; houses Detroit Tamburitza Orchestra (class 1957 under Andy Benda, first concert June 13 1959, renamed DTO ~1977), Detroit Star Junior Tamburitzans (first appearance 1972, dir. Ken Kosovec) and Croatian Folklore Ensemble 'Nova Nada'. Annual DTO spring concert (Apr 27 2024).

organizations.name: Rastko Serbian Folklore Group (St. Stevan Decanski, St. Petka Vratnica, Holy Ascension)
organizations.notes: Grew out of 'Mladost' shared with St. Dimitrije church in Windsor; 60+ dancers in 3 age groups; Friday practices (page last updated ~2020). Ravanica (St. Lazarus Cathedral, Detroit) also runs youth kolo groups.

organizations.name: Finnish Center Association
organizations.notes: Center at 35200 W. Eight Mile, Farmington Hills dedicated 1974; 500+ core members; ensembles: Soittoniekat/FinnFolk (woodwinds, strings, accordion), Finnish American Singers of Michigan, Nordic Heritage Folk Dancers.

organizations.name: Hungarian Arts Club
organizations.notes: White Rose debutante ball; also Hungarian American Cultural Center (Taylor) and the Csipke Ensemble (Detroit/Toledo Hungarian folk dance).

organizations.name: Sarisan Slovak Folk Ensemble
organizations.notes: Founded and still directed by Milan Straka.

organizations.name: Hamazkayin Arax Dance Ensemble (Hamazkayin Detroit chapter)
organizations.notes: Choreographer Nayiri Karapetian; annual concert drew 400+ (Nov 2024).

organizations.name: Maltese American Benevolent Society (Corktown) and Maltese American Community Club (Dearborn)
organizations.notes: Festa il-Vitorja; rabbit dinners, St. Paul's Feast, Miss Malta pageant.

organizations.name: North American Indian Association of Detroit (NAIA)
organizations.notes: Began as the North American Indian Club in the 1940s (NPS); organized the 2025 Hart Plaza powwow (exec. dir. Brian Moore; program dir. Travis Schuyler).

organizations.name: American Indian Health and Family Services (AIHFS)
organizations.notes: Runs annual 'Pow Wow in the D'.

organizations.name: Caribbean Cultural and Carnival Organization (CCCO)
organizations.notes: Umbrella of island groups; Detroit Caribbean Cultural Festival & parade.

organizations.name: Mexican Patriotic Committee of Metro Detroit (MPC)
organizations.notes: Cinco de Mayo Parade & Fiesta.

organizations.name: Ballet Folklorico de Detroit (BFD)
organizations.notes: Founded by Lance Rodriguez (with Janette Rodriguez); 'one of Michigan's largest volunteer-run folklorico groups'; affordable classes; annual holiday concert at Senate Theater; 7,400 FB followers.

organizations.name: TeMaTe Institute for Black Dance and Culture
organizations.notes: Director Ajara Alghali; weekly African dance classes with drums at 3000 Fenkell; annual October Convening.

organizations.name: Detroit Blues Society
organizations.notes: Maintains open-jam list; 'Blues Notes' newsletter; 2006 'Best Blues Society' (Blues Foundation KBA).

organizations.name: Great Lakes Taiko Center
organizations.notes: Novi; Godaiko Drummers and Tanoshii Taiko Tai community group; MI Bon festival since 2021.

organizations.name: Great Lakes Aradhana Committee (GLAC)
organizations.notes: Carnatic and Hindustani concerts, Tyagaraja Aradhana; 30+ events/yr per web summary (unverified). Also Komal Rishabh Music Society (Hindustani) and Bharatiya Temple, Troy.

organizations.name: Celtic pipe bands: St. Andrew's Pipe Band, Michigan Scottish Pipes and Drums, Celtic Pipes and Drums
organizations.notes: Michigan Scottish P&D founded 1980 by P/M William O'Donnell (Grade 4, teaching band); Celtic Pipes and Drums practice most Tuesdays 6:30-8:30 at First United Methodist, Troy; St. Andrew's band weekly at Kilgour.

organizations.name: Michigan Traditional Arts Program (MSU Museum) - Michigan Heritage Awards
organizations.notes: MHA established 1985: plaque, legislative tribute, $1,000 stipend; 147 awardees listed through 2026, 43 of them in the Detroit MSA. Also runs Michigan Traditional Arts Apprenticeships.

organizations.name: Harmonie Society (Gesang-Verein Harmonie)
organizations.notes: Chartered 1852; records 1881-1993 at the Bentley.

organizations.name: Ford Motor Company Music Department
organizations.notes: Defunct 1947.

organizations.name: Detroit Musicians Association
organizations.notes: Founded the Hackley Collection at DPL (1943).

organizations.name: Detroit Country Dance Society
organizations.notes: Co-hosted Starry Night from 1995; current status not verified in this thread.

organizations.name: Olde Michigan Ruffwater Stringband
organizations.notes: Still playing Ann Arbor contras per AACTMAD's musician page.

organizations.name: Ann Arbor Council (now Community) for Traditional Music and Dance (AACTMAD)
organizations.notes: Founding year 1975 from a museum directory (low confidence).

organizations.name: The Ark
organizations.notes: About 400 seats, 300+ shows a year; owns its 316 S. Main home since 2012.

organizations.name: Detroit Folk School
organizations.notes: Absorbed the Detroit Square Dance Society in Jan 2025; runs Detroit Queer Square Dance, the Detroit Cantastoria Festival and old-time workshops (Brittany Haas, Nic Gareiss, Hubby Jenkins in 2026).

festivals.name: Motor City Irish Fest
festivals.notes: Greenmead Historical Park, Livonia; June 12-14 2026. WXYZ called the 2025 edition the 15th annual (so founded about 2011). | 15th annual June 6-8, 2025; two stages, Irish dance schools; adult tickets $10 online / $15 gate (2025).

festivals.name: Detroit Highland Games (St. Andrew's Society)
festivals.notes: 177th Games Aug 1, 2026 at Greenmead Historical Park, Livonia, with a Friday-night ceilidh. Claims the longest continuous Highland Games in North America since 1849 (the Society's founding year; first Games date unverified). Past sites: Belle Isle, University of Detroit, Historic Fort Wayne, Ford House, Ford Field.

festivals.name: Paint Creek Folklore Society Tin Whistle Concert
festivals.notes: 53rd annual on Nov 14 2026 (RFD Boys), $20. Founded year inferred from the 53rd edition and PCFS's 1974 founding.

festivals.name: A Starry Night for a Ramble (benefit contra & square dance)
festivals.notes: PCFS + OCTDS (since 1997); Paint Creek Country Dance Orchestra (since 1985); began in Pontiac 1984, moved through Waterford, Royal Oak, Clawson to Troy. Cancelled 2021-23 and Feb 2025; held Feb 10 2024 and May 16 2026. $10, under 12 free.

festivals.name: KlezMitten Michigan Klezmer Festival
festivals.notes: International Institute, Midtown Detroit; 2nd edition Sep 7 2025 with seven bands (Heartland Klezmorim, Klezmephonic, Klezundheit, Schmaltz, 7Layers, Klezmer Academy, Chutzpah). 2026 edition not confirmed.

festivals.name: Apple Blossom Bliss (contra weekend)
festivals.notes: Ann Arbor, Concourse Hall; May 8 2026, May 7 2027.

festivals.name: Melt into Spring (dance weekend)
festivals.notes: Ann Arbor; Mar 27 2026, Apr 16 2027.

festivals.name: Fenton Bluegrass Festival
festivals.notes: Genesee County (Flint MSA); free first edition in Rackham Park, Oct 2026. | First annual Oct 19, 2026; promoted by the Southeast Michigan Bluegrass Music Association.

festivals.name: Detroit Folk Festival
festivals.notes: Started by Audra Kubat at the Trumbullplex collective (Woodbridge), 'six years' before 2018. 2018: noon-11pm at the Old Miami, 25 artists, $7/$10, half the proceeds to InsideOut Literary Arts. Relaunched Sep 26 2026 'as a yearly gathering' in the backyard garden of A Detroit House of Music: '26+ songwriters in rounds', BYOB, bonfire, DJ at midnight. Lineup included Lac La Belle, Jo Serrapere, Chris Bathgate, Joe Reilly, jessica Care moore, Mahogany Jones.

festivals.name: Woodbridge Porch Concerts
festivals.notes: 6th annual Oct 10 2026, free, 12-6pm across front porches; started during the pandemic (WDET, Oct 6 2026). Folk among the styles.

festivals.name: Divinity United Gospel Quartet Showcase
festivals.notes: See recurring_events. 2026 edition unverified.

festivals.name: Concert of Colors
festivals.notes: Founded by Ismael Ahmed; 35th annual July 15-19 2026 included his celebration of life. World/heritage music; detail in the heritage thread. Founding year inferred from the '35th annual' in 2026 (could be 1993). | Founded by Ismael Ahmed (ACCESS) with New Detroit, one day at Chene Park; 9 days by 2019; 2026 = 5 days, 13 Midtown venues, free, Smithsonian Folklife partnership. Ahmed died 2026. Edition numbering disagrees: WDET called 2025 the 34th, organizers call 2026 the 35th anniversary (1993 + 33 years).

festivals.name: Ypsi-Arbor All-Day Sing (Sacred Harp)
festivals.notes: 1st annual Oct 3 2026, 10am-3pm with potluck, the Saturday before the first Sunday in October.

festivals.name: Arab International Festival (Warren Ave, Dearborn)
festivals.attendance: ~250,000 over 3 days (Metromode); 'about three times Dearborn's population' (Arab American News)
festivals.notes: Ran 1995-2012; shut down by the American Arab Chamber of Commerce after protests by anti-Muslim groups made it a costly liability.

festivals.name: Cinco de Mayo Parade & Fiesta (Mexican Patriotic Committee of Metro Detroit)
festivals.notes: 61st annual in 2026 (May 2-3), 2.4-mile route on W. Vernor Hwy from Patton Park to Clark Park; folklorico and mariachi at fiesta. Founding year inferred from '61st annual' (medium). Called the largest such parade in Michigan (Latino USA 2017).

festivals.name: Hamtramck Labor Day Festival
festivals.notes: Two stages on Joseph Campau; historically capped by the Polish Day Parade until the parade left for Warren in 2022. Music lineup is now mostly rock/rap/soul (Metro Times 2025).

festivals.name: Polish Day Parade
festivals.notes: Began 'in the 1930s on Belle Isle', then Jefferson Ave downtown, then Joseph Campau in Hamtramck on Labor Day; moved to Warren in 2022 (fifth year in Warren in 2026, Aug 29). Founding year approximate.

festivals.name: Paczki Day (Fat Tuesday) in Hamtramck
festivals.notes: Bar-hopping party with polka; the parody polka-rock band The Polish Muslims plays multiple halls (Ant Hall 10:30am etc.). American Polish Century Club (Sterling Heights) runs a Polish-music Paczki party ($5-7, 2026).

festivals.name: American Polish Festival (American Polish Century Club)
festivals.notes: Sterling Heights; 'finest Polish dance ensembles in Michigan' plus polka bands.

festivals.name: Greektown Heritage Festival
festivals.notes: Free; Greek dancing, lamb roast, live music on Monroe St. Returned July 25 2026 after a one-year pause.

festivals.name: Ya'ssoo Greek Festival (St. George Greek Orthodox)
festivals.notes: Bloomfield Hills; parish youth dance troupes. One of several parish festivals (Nativity of the Virgin Mary, Plymouth: michigangreekfestival.com).

festivals.name: Detroit Greek Independence Day Parade
festivals.notes: Greektown.

festivals.name: Armenia Fest (Metro Detroit Armenia Fest Committee + Detroit Knights of Vartan)
festivals.notes: Royal Oak Farmers Market; free; 17th year in 2025 (founding inferred); Armenia Fest Allstar Band (dir. Vaughn Masropian) and Hamazkayin Arax Dance Ensemble.

festivals.name: Festa il-Vitorja (Maltese American Benevolent Society)
festivals.notes: 15th annual in 2024; Mass at Most Holy Trinity then festa at the society's Corktown club.

festivals.name: Pow Wow in the D (American Indian Health and Family Services)
festivals.notes: Annual AIHFS powwow; at Wayne State University intramural field since 2024 (May 17 2025).

festivals.name: Indigenous Peoples' Day Powwow at Hart Plaza
festivals.notes: Oct 13 2025: first downtown powwow in 30+ years; City of Detroit (Councilwoman Gabriella Santiago-Romero) with NAIA, AIHFS, South Eastern Michigan Indians, Detroit Indigenous Peoples Alliance. 2026 edition not verified.

festivals.name: African World Festival (Charles H. Wright Museum)
festivals.notes: Hart Plaza, July 10-12 2026; $15 admission 2026; 100+ vendors. Founding year from web summary (medium).

festivals.name: Detroit Caribbean Cultural Festival & Carnival (CCCO)
festivals.notes: CCCO formed January 1979; 2025 festival Aug 23 at Marygrove Conservancy; has also run a Caribbean parade/lawn party within Concert of Colors at the DIA.

festivals.name: Bangladeshi Festival / Hamtramck Diversity Festival (Bangladesh Association of Michigan)
festivals.notes: On Conant ('Bangladesh Avenue'); local Bangladeshi bands plus a visiting pop star; serves ~20,000 Bangladeshis in Hamtramck and adjacent Detroit. 2009 = first per 'second year in a row' in 2010.

festivals.name: Michigan Hmong New Year (United Hmong of Michigan)
festivals.notes: Nov 22-23 2025, Elite Sportsplex, Waterford (Oakland County). Qeej and kwv txhiaj presented at the DIA's 'Hmong Cultural Journey'.

festivals.name: Japan Festival (Japan Business Society of Detroit)
festivals.notes: Novi High School, Oct 4 2026; taiko (Godaiko Drummers), Sakura instrumental group, tea ceremony.

festivals.name: MI Bon Summer Festival (Great Lakes Taiko Center)
festivals.notes: Participatory Bon odori with taiko, Novi; first held Aug 7 2021.

festivals.name: Detroit Chinatown Block Party
festivals.notes: Second annual July 25 2026 (Cass Corridor's former Chinatown).

festivals.name: Rastko Winter Dance Festival (Serbian folklore)
festivals.notes: Hosted by St. Stevan Decanski Serbian Orthodox Church, Warren; draws youth kolo groups from Indiana etc. Date of freshest evidence not established (low).

festivals.name: Csipke Tabor (Hungarian folk dance and music camp)
festivals.notes: Run by Detroit/Toledo's Csipke Ensemble and the Detroit Hungarian community at Sauk Valley Resort (Jackson County); June 22-29 2024.

festivals.name: Celtic Festival (mi-celtic.org)
festivals.notes: '30th Celtic Festival July 9-10 2027' (founding inferred); DIMA instrument petting zoo, Purcell Irish Pipers of Detroit, Gaelic League set dancers on its schedule. Location not stated in fetched text; believed to be Saline (Washtenaw) - unverified.

festivals.name: Ann Arbor Folk Festival (The Ark)
festivals.place: Hill Auditorium, Ann Arbor (Power Center in 1976, Michigan Theater 1982)
festivals.notes: The Ark's largest fundraiser. The Ark lists the 1st as 1976 and the 2nd as 1979; many secondary sources say 1977 (disagreement). 49th held Jan 2026; 50th set for Jan 29-30, 2027 with Jeff Daniels as emcee. Two nights; Hill Auditorium seats roughly 3,500 (attendance figure not published; low confidence).

festivals.name: Michigan State Championship Old-Time Fiddlers Contest (Huron Township Applefest)
festivals.notes: Since 2006 (director Jim McKinney) contestants play a waltz, schottische, jig and reel for blind judges, with points for Michigan repertoire; state-champion title recognized by governors since 1997. The Applefest itself continues (Yelp, 2026), but the contest's current status was not confirmed.

festivals.name: Henry Ford-era fiddle contests (Ford-dealer contests, 'Henry Ford Gold Cup')
festivals.place: Ford dealerships (TN, KY, southern IN); claimed finals in Detroit/Dearborn
festivals.notes: Contested history: popular accounts (e.g., homewood.net) say Ford sponsored contests including a 'Henry Ford Gold Cup' in Dearborn; Paul Gifford's archival study (J. Soc. American Music, 2010) concludes Ford never sponsored any fiddle contest and the national contest is a myth stemming from Uncle Bunt Stephens.

festivals.name: Festival of Michigan Folklife
festivals.notes: 1987-1998 (hiatus 1997); 75+ tradition bearers; became the National Folk Festival 1999-2001.

festivals.name: Great Lakes Folk Festival
festivals.notes: 2002-2017, free; 4-5 stages and ~100 performers at peak; ~$2M annual local economic impact claimed. Hiatus became permanent after 2017.

festivals.name: Red Cedar Roots Festival
festivals.notes: Inaugural Aug 14-15, 2026, explicitly reviving the Great Lakes Folk Festival legacy after a two-year study committee.

festivals.name: Wheatland Music Festival
festivals.attendance: about 10,000-14,000 (low confidence; 2025 'more than 12,000' per a Facebook summary)
festivals.notes: First held Aug 24, 1974 as a benefit for the Mt. Pleasant Food Co-op on the Rhode farm; several hundred attended. A Detroit Folk School 'Wheatland TAW field trip' (2026) shows the Detroit scene's tie to it.

festivals.name: Thumbfest
festivals.place: Lexington (Sanilac County, just north of St. Clair County)
festivals.notes: Listed by Local Spins for Sept 5-6, 2025; folk/acoustic. Founding year not found.

festivals.name: Crossroads Ceili
festivals.notes: Two nights each December bringing Mick Gavin's students and family together; 2024-2026 evidence not checked.

festivals.name: Galactic Steam Dulcimer Circus
festivals.notes: Nov 13, 1976 convention-style dulcimer gathering organized by Eddie Damm; an impromptu contra called by Dale Johnson there seeded the Oakland County contra scene. Unknown whether it recurred.

radio.notes: Sun 1-3pm. Syndicated singer-songwriter show produced in Ann Arbor, heard on 125 stations. Added to WDET in Dec 2009, the same week WDET cut its local roots shows. This is the only regular folk-leaning program on Detroit's NPR station.
Tue 9-10pm, local artists of all genres, often folk/Americana (e.g. Laurel Premo, Whiskey Charmers). Part of the Feb 2024 local-music revamp.
Sat 5-7pm world music. Its status after Ahmed's death is not confirmed.

radio.show: The Roots Music Project + Roots Break
radio.host: Bob Nolan (from Sep 11 2026; previously Jeremy Baldwin)
radio.notes: Sat 4-7pm plus Fri noon-2pm: bluegrass, blues, country, gospel, folk. Station serves Ann Arbor and Detroit.
Sun 6-8pm, Saturday repeat. Watroba's 40th year on radio (started WDET 1986); Folk DJ Hall of Fame 2019.

radio.show: Urban gospel format, 'The Voice of the Church in Detroit'
radio.notes: Founded by Dr. Haley Bell and Dr. Wendell Cox; first broadcast Nov 7 1956 from Inkster (on 1440); first Black-owned-and-operated station built from the ground up.
Sun 1-3pm from the Gaelic League (seen in Oct 2026 event listing). Low confidence.
Thu 10:30-noon roots/folk 'from both sides of the river'. CJAM called Brown its 'former host' in 2023; current status unknown.

archives.name: Walter P. Reuther Library, Wayne State University: Wayne State Folklore Archive materials

James Papers; Folklore Archive Student Field Projects Records, card files by ethnicity), the MSU Museum and the Great Lakes Lighthouse Keepers Association.

archives.name: Detroit Public Library: E. Azalia Hackley Collection of African Americans in the Performing Arts

archives.name: Bentley Historical Library, University of Michigan (outside MSA)
archives.notes: Gertrude P. Kurath recordings of Native American songs 1953-54 (Great Lakes dance documentation); Harmonie Society of Detroit records 1881-1993; Mamie Connor diaries and McCreery papers (cited for Ford dances); Detroit Jewish News digital archive. archives.name: UM-Flint Karl Byarski Collection, 1953-1996 (outside MSA)

archives.name: Michigan Fiddle (michiganfiddle.com)
archives.notes: Community archive of Michigan fiddle history: county-history quotations on French fiddling, fiddler bios (Pattee, Bisbee), Gifford commentaries, the Byarski collection, contest history.

archives.name: Square Dance History Project

timeline.event: Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac founds Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit (July 24) with French settlers and allied Huron/Wyandot, Odawa and Potawatomi nations; Ste. Anne's parish founded July 26, 1701 (2nd-oldest continuously operating Catholic parish in the US). No specific record of Indigenous or habitant music from 1701 was found.

Detroit passes to Britain (surrendered 1760, ceded 1763) but stays culturally French with heavy Native influence into the early 1800s; French 'ribbon farms' line the river from the town to Grosse Pointe and along the St. Clair River.

Judge James May (in Detroit 1778-1830) recalls weekly or fortnightly 'Detroit assemblies' and dancing at the river farmhouses 'not more than four arpents apart, from the city to Grosse Point': 'A fiddle was in every house'.

Visitor Wm. C. Hoyt finds four languages spoken (French, English, Scotch, Indian) and attends a French dance in a one-story hut (whisky 3 cents a glass) where a Black fiddler calls 'Up here! down there! cross over! all hands around!'. By 1890 he wrote that 'the French dancing parties have fallen through the trap door'.
Mariners' Church of Detroit founded; it later became the 'Maritime Sailors' Cathedral' of Lightfoot's song.
Dancing master Adam Couse (1810-1885) opens Detroit's first music store; Stephen Foster dedicated a ballad to him in 1850.
St. Andrew's Society of Detroit founded; it dates its Highland Games to the same year.

St. Andrew's Society of Detroit founded and its Highland Games begin (claimed as the longest continuous Highland Games in North America). The same year German immigrants found the Gesang-Verein Harmonie singing society.

Couse publishes the 'Detroit Schottisch', reportedly selling about 100,000 copies; Paul Gifford considers it the likely source of the old-time standard 'Flop-Eared Mule' (others say the tunes share a common ancestor).
Early 1870s: first Middle Eastern (mostly Christian Lebanese) settlers arrive in Detroit.
1880s: O. F. 'Cub' Berdan publishes dance music in Detroit, including the 'Grace Waltz' named for his daughter (per fiddler Jim Moran via Paul Gifford).
Michigan Malleable Iron opens in Delray, drawing Hungarians who build Detroit's Hungarian enclave.

Civil War veteran fiddler John A. Pattee of New Boston (Wayne County) forms the vaudeville act 'Old Soldier Fiddlers' of Union and Confederate veterans; he died in Dec 1924 as a favorite of WEAF's radio barn dance.
Ford factories employ 555 'Syrian' workers; Henry Ford's $5 day pulls Macedonians, Finns, Romanians and Arabs to Detroit.
Gaelic League of Detroit founded (Dec); by 1920 Detroit also has the largest Romanian population in the Midwest.
Gaelic League of Detroit founded (first at Grand River and Rosa Parks; at 2068 Michigan Ave in Corktown since the early 1950s); centenary celebrated 2020-22.

Henry Ford and Thomas Edison 'discover' 80-year-old dance fiddler Jasper 'Jep' Bisbee (Paris, Mich.) and Ford sends him in his private car to record for Edison (NYT, Nov 24, 1923), one of the first rural fiddle recordings.

Ford founds the Ford Motor Company Music Department: staff on the company payroll who for 23 years played for dances, taught throughout Michigan and promoted 'old-fashioned dancing' nationally. Dancing master Benjamin Lovett comes to Dearborn (The Henry Ford says 1924; another account says 1928) and cimbalom player William 'Billy' Hallup is hired.

Cape Breton fiddler John A. 'Johnny Archie' MacDonald moves to Detroit, becomes a Detroit police officer, and for half a century sponsors dances, concerts and house sessions that keep Cape Breton music alive in the Motor City.

June: the Ford-owned Dearborn Independent's 'Return of the Dance' frames Ford's revival in racialized terms ('a rational and racially American character'); reprinted as 'Henry Ford Shakes a Wicked Hoof' in Literary Digest.
Dec 11: Maine fiddler Mellie Dunham, brought by Pullman car, plays for Ford's party in Dearborn; Ford had invited 38 fiddlers before him but none drew comparable press. Dunham goes on to vaudeville.

Jan 1926: Ford dealers in Tennessee, Kentucky and southern Indiana stage fiddle contests (a last-minute fix when a broadcast could not reach Cincinnati). Uncle Bunt Stephens then claims to have won a national Ford contest in Detroit; Paul Gifford's archival research says Ford never sponsored any fiddle contest and the 'national contest' is a myth.

Dearborn Publishing Co. issues 'Good Morning: After a Sleep of Twenty-five Years, Old-fashioned Dancing is Being Revived by Mr. and Mrs. Henry Ford', with dance descriptions by Mr. and Mrs. Benjamin Lovett. Henry Ford's Old Time / Old Fashioned Dance Orchestra records 1925-27 (e.g., 'A Southern Schottische', Columbia 555-D, recorded Jan 16, 1926).

Ford's orchestra and Lovett visit Detroit schools, including Lincoln, then the city's only Black school (photo, 1928). Gifford found Black fiddlers Ed and John Campbell of Dresden, Ontario, were invited to play with Ford's orchestra.
Teenage Russell Street Usher Board Four forms at Russell Street Baptist; it becomes the Flying Clouds of Detroit, the state's leading jubilee quartet of the 1940s.
Ford's Edison Institute (Greenfield Village) Schools open with dancing in the curriculum; Lovett is superintendent 1929-1936.
1930s: Polish Day Parade begins on Belle Isle.

Oct 26: Lovett Hall ballroom dedicated in Dearborn; Henry and Clara Ford lead the dancing as Ford's Old Time Orchestra plays waltzes and quadrilles, with Lovett calling for 300 guests. Monthly dances followed.
Alan Lomax records in Detroit for the Library of Congress (Delta blues by Calvin Frazier and Sampson Pittman; Serbian-Americans near the Chrysler plant).

Alan Lomax's Library of Congress Michigan expedition (about 250 discs, 8 reels of film). In Detroit: Aug 5 Serbian gusle epics (Pajo Tomić) and Romanian/Serbian tamburitza; Aug 8 Hungarian songs in Delray; Nov 1 Delta blues by Calvin Frazier and Sampson Pittman plus Frazier family gospel. The LOC tags 116 online items to Detroit (52 sound recordings, 64 card-catalog entries).
Wayne State University Folklore Archive founded by English professors Emelyn Gardner and Thelma James, later called the oldest and largest record of urban folk traditions in the US.
1940s: North American Indian Club (later Association) organized.

John Lee Hooker takes a job with Ford Motor Company in Detroit and frequents the clubs of Hastings Street. Same year the Detroit Musicians Association founds the E. Azalia Hackley Collection at the Detroit Public Library.

Ford's 'Early American Dance Music' half-hour radio program (Lovett calling, Ford Early American Orchestra, broadcast from Ford's Engineering Laboratory) ends when civilian car production resumes. Lovett retires in 1944.
Jack and Devora Brown found Fortune Records in Detroit (1946-1995), recording hillbilly, blues, R&B and doo-wop.
Flying Clouds record 'Something Within Me' for John W. Gilbert's Detroit label Religious Recordings.
Henry Ford dies; the Music Department's 23-year run ends.
John Lee Hooker records 'Boogie Chillen'' at United Sound Systems, Detroit (Sept 1948; released Nov 1948 on Modern).
WDET first broadcast (Feb 13).
Entire Ukrainian Bandurist Chorus (17 families) immigrates from DP camps, settling in Hamtramck.

The Ukrainian Bandurist Chorus, displaced since WWII, immigrates as a single artistic unit (sponsored by Sol Hurok and Detroit lawyer John Panchuk); most of its 17 families settle in Hamtramck. It becomes a 2025 NEA National Heritage Fellow.

Casey Clark's Lazy Ranch Boys take over WJR's Saturday 'Big Barn Frolic' at the Dairyworkers Hall in Highland Park, moving within a year to UAW hall 12101 Mack Ave (weekly barn dance 1952-1957, stage shows then square and round dances). Gov. G. Mennen 'Soapy' Williams calls a square dance from that stage c. 1955.

Jan-Nov: bluegrass pioneers the Lonesome Pine Fiddlers are based in Detroit on WJR and the Big Barn Frolic. Jan 31: the Five MacDonald Fiddlers (Cape Breton expatriates incl. composer Dan R. MacDonald) photographed at a Detroit concert. A Wayne State survey ranks 'hillbillies' and 'poor Southern whites' tied with criminals as Detroit's most 'undesirable' people.
Wieliczka (Dearborn), oldest surviving Polish folk dance group, founded.
WCHB, the first Black-owned and operated station built from the ground up, signs on from Inkster (Nov 7).
Tamburica class at Northern High School under Andy Benda becomes the Detroit Senior Tamburitzans (first concert June 13 1959), later the Detroit Tamburitza Orchestra.
Mattie Moss Clark's first composition; she directs at Bailey Cathedral COGIC and shapes the mass-choir sound.
Ukrainian American Archives & Museum and Hungarian Arts Club founded.
Late 1950s-early 1960s: Black Bottom and its Paradise Valley/Hastings Street entertainment district demolished for Lafayette Park and the I-75 freeway.
Belle and Herb Cohen open the Raven Gallery coffeehouse on James Couzens in Detroit (later at 12 Mile & Greenfield, Southfield), presenting Josh White Sr. and Jr. and the Dorothy Ashby Trio monthly.

Michigan chess champion Morrie Widenbaum opens the Chess Mate on Livernois near the University of Detroit (200 capacity, no alcohol); Bobby Fischer plays 51 boards there in 1964; the club turns to folk and blues (Gordon Lightfoot, Doc Watson, Buffy Sainte-Marie, Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Phil Ochs, Rev. Gary Davis).
The Retort folk coffeehouse operates in the Mount Royal Hotel on Woodward (1964 schedule with harpist Dorothy Ashby, who also hosted a Detroit folk radio show).
The Ark opens in Ann Arbor.
Wawel, the first adult Polish folk dance group, founded; Cinco de Mayo parade tradition starts about now (61st in 2026).

June 19: Joni Anderson marries Detroit-area folksinger Chuck Mitchell at his parents' home in Rochester, Mich.; as 'Detroit's favorite folk singers' they live at the Verona (Ferry & Cass) and Joni plays 60+ Chess Mate dates in 12 months and writes 'The Circle Game' in Detroit. Separately, four Ann Arbor churches found The Ark coffeehouse (Dec 1965).
Finnish Center Association founded (center dedicated 1974).
Folk clubs Chess Mate (Livernois near 6 Mile), Living End, Retort, Raven Gallery (Southfield); Joni and Chuck Mitchell work the Chess Mate.
GMWA (founded 1967 by Rev. James Cleveland in Detroit) holds its first board meeting (March) and first national convention (summer, King Solomon Church) in Detroit.
Sarisan Slovak Folk Ensemble founded by Milan Straka.
Chess Mate closes (Free Press account; some sources say 1973); Widenbaum dies a year later at 46. The building is now a laundromat.

Burt Schwartz becomes the Detroit-area contact for the Country Dance and Song Society. Howard 'Louie Bluie' Armstrong, a Black string-band fiddler living in Detroit since WWII, reunites with Carl Martin and Ted Bogan.
Paint Creek Folklore Society founded in Rochester, Oakland County (50th anniversary year 2024). First Wheatland Bluegrass Festival held Aug 24, 1974 near Remus (outside the metro).
Edmund Fitzgerald sinks (Nov 10); Mariners' Church rings its bell 29 times. Lightfoot later changes 'musty old hall' to 'rustic'.
Clare-born fiddler and melodeon player Mick Gavin settles in Detroit, later starting multiple sessions and mentoring a generation of Irish players.
Psarianos Violins founded.

Nov 13: the 'Galactic Steam Dulcimer Circus' at the Detroit Historical Museum, where caller Dale Johnson leads an impromptu contra with the jamming musicians, the Paint Creek members' first taste of contra. The Ark launches the Ann Arbor Folk Festival as a fundraiser (The Ark dates the 1st festival to 1976; many sources say 1977).

Dec: Burt Schwartz and Paul Tyler start the Detroit Country Dance Society; Sept 26, 1978 the Olde Michigan Ruffwater Stringband forms out of Paint Creek; May 1979 DCDS starts a monthly Saturday contra and square dance at St. Timothy's Church, Detroit.
Ukrainian Cultural Center (Warren) and American Indian Health & Family Services open.
Caribbean Cultural and Carnival Organization formed.
About 1979-80 the Raven closes, leaving metro folk fans to drive to Ann Arbor or East Lansing (1991 Detroit Jewish News account).
Trinity House Theatre founded by Trinity Baptist Church members in Livonia.
African World Festival begins (Charles H. Wright Museum).
Feb 11: first 'Starry Night for a Ramble' community contra dance (Bethany Baptist, Pontiac). Oct 2: Judi Morningstar writes 'March of St. Timothy' for the DCDS church dance.
Michigan Heritage Awards established; first Detroit honorees Sippie Wallace and Thelma James.
Matt Watroba starts 'Folks Like Us' on WDET (November).

Michigan is featured at the Smithsonian Festival of American Folklife, and MSU folklorists stage the first Festival of Michigan Folklife in East Lansing (75+ musicians, storytellers and craftspeople).
Howard 'Louie Bluie' Armstrong (Detroit) named NEA National Heritage Fellow.
Howard Armstrong becomes an NEA National Heritage Fellow (Detroit), the metro's only fiddler so honored found; Nadim Dlaikan (Lebanese nay, Southgate) follows in 2002.
MAMA's Coffeehouse first show (May).
Concert of Colors founded by Ismael Ahmed at Chene Park; Rastko Serbian folklore group formed.
Rob Reinhart launches Acoustic Café in Ann Arbor.
Arab International Festival on Warren Ave, Dearborn begins (to 2012).
Trinity House switches from theatre to live music.

The Wayne State Folklore Archive is disassembled and dispersed to the Reuther Library, the MSU Museum and the Great Lakes Lighthouse Keepers Association. East Lansing hosts the National Folk Festival (1999-2001).
Nadim Dlaikan named NEA Heritage Fellow; Maples Arabic Music Ensemble founded in a Dearborn public elementary school.
Great Lakes Folk Festival begins in East Lansing (runs 2002-2017, peaking at 4-5 stages and ~100 performers).
Garfield House Concerts (Northville) begins.
WDET format change brings the first cancellation of Folks Like Us; WEMU carries it until it returns to WDET.
BaseLine Folk Society starts in Plymouth (inferred from '12th season' in 2016).
Arab American National Museum opens (May 5); Hamazkayin Arax Armenian dance ensemble founded.
WDET cancels Folks Like Us (23 years), Arkansas Traveler and Deep River; adds Acoustic Café (December).
National Arab Orchestra's first concert (Apr 4, Ann Arbor); first Bangladeshi Festival in Hamtramck.
Motor City Irish Fest begins (15th annual June 6-8, 2025 at Greenmead, Livonia).
Audra Kubat starts the Detroit Folk Festival at the Trumbullplex (year inferred); Detroit Music Teachers Collective founded.
Last Arab International Festival; shut down after anti-Muslim protest groups made it a liability.
Ballet Folklorico de Detroit founded.
Otus Supply's Parliament Room opens in Ferndale (December).
Watroba moves his folk show to WKAR (October).
Detroit Folk Festival at the Old Miami: 25 artists, songwriters in the round.
Mick Gavin (Redford) receives a Michigan Heritage Award for Irish fiddling; Neil Woodward (Howell, Livingston Co.) is honored for Michigan traditional music and storytelling.
Common Chords founded by Robert Jones and Matt Watroba.
Detroit Institute of Music Education closes after six years.
COVID: The Ark closes to the public in March 2020 (folk festival goes online in Jan 2021; in-person reopening July 29, 2021); Paint Creek/OCTDS 'Starry Night' contra dance cancelled 2021-2023.
Woodbridge Porch Concerts start during the pandemic (6th edition in 2026).
First MI Bon dance festival (Great Lakes Taiko Center, Novi).
Polish Day Parade leaves Hamtramck for Warren; Ukrainian refugees arrive (nearly 100 children at a Warren Ukrainian Catholic school).
Otus Supply / Parliament Room closes abruptly (Feb 27).
WDET adds six local evening music shows (Feb 5); first Motown Museum gospel quartet showcase (Jul 27).

Feb 10: Starry Night for a Ramble returns at First United Methodist, Troy ($10), in Paint Creek Folklore Society's 50th year. The Detroit Square Dance Society holds queer potluck square dances at Vámonos in Southwest Detroit.
Rev. Robert Jones receives the Michigan Heritage Award (Jun 14); Edmund Fitzgerald 50th-anniversary events at Mariners' Church (Nov 7-10).
American Indian Services closes after 49 years (July); Ukrainian Bandurist Chorus named NEA Heritage Fellows; first downtown powwow in 30+ years at Hart Plaza (Oct 13).

Jan: Detroit Square Dance Society becomes part of the new Detroit Folk School; Pride Source runs 'How a Queer Collective in Detroit Is Dancing on Henry Ford's Grave' (Jan 3). The Ark marks its 60th anniversary; the Ukrainian Bandurist Chorus is named an NEA National Heritage Fellow; Rev. Robert Jones (Detroit, blues) gets a Michigan Heritage Award.
Ismael Ahmed dies (Jan 31); Watroba's 50/40 concert at The Ark (Jun 28); Bob Nolan takes over WEMU Roots (Sep 11); Detroit Folk Festival relaunched (Sep 26); first Ypsi-Arbor All-Day Sing (Oct 3).
Concert of Colors runs first festival without founder Ismael Ahmed, with a Smithsonian Folklife partnership; Polish Weekly census counts 601 Polish folk dance students.

Jan 30-31: 49th Ann Arbor Folk Fest at Hill Auditorium; Feb-Mar: Detroit Folk School brings Hubby Jenkins, Brittany Haas and Nic Gareiss; Aug 1: 177th St. Andrew's Highland Games at Greenmead, Livonia; Aug 14-15: Red Cedar Roots Festival revives the Great Lakes Folk Festival legacy in East Lansing; Sept: lineup announced for the 50th Ann Arbor Folk Festival (Jan 29-30, 2027; Jeff Daniels emcee).

tunes_named_for_city.title: Detroit (The Sacred Harp 39t)
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Music attributed to 'Bradshaw, 1820', words by Philip Doddridge (1755). Sung at the 2025 United Convention in Atlanta, though no Detroit group sings it at home.

tunes_named_for_city.title: The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald (Lightfoot, 1976)
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Names the Detroit church ('in a musty old hall in Detroit they prayed'), later sung as 'rustic'.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Detroit Schottische (Detroit Schottisch)
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Adam Couse, Detroit, 1854; in Elias Howe's Musician's Omnibus No. 1 (1863) as part of the 'May Flower Schottische Quadrilles'. Gifford thinks 'Flop-Eared Mule' derives from it; WOTFA argues for a shared ancestor instead.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Flop-Eared Mule (Lop-Eared Mule)
tunes_named_for_city.notes: A Southern standard with a possible Detroit parlor-dance ancestor (see above). Contested.

tunes_named_for_city.title: The Detroit (Detroit Jig)
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Jig recorded by Natalie MacMaster on 'My Roots Are Showing' (set with 'The Mucking of Geordie's Byre' and Dan R. MacDonald's 'The Boys of the Lake'); composer not found. thesession.org tune 10509.

tunes_named_for_city.title: The Five Fiddlers
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Honors the Detroit-formed Five MacDonald Fiddlers.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Little Judique Jig
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Traditional; first recorded by Detroit police officer Johnny Archie MacDonald.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Sweetness of Mary
tunes_named_for_city.notes: By Joan MacDonald Boes, pianist of the Detroit-based Five MacDonald Fiddlers.

tunes_named_for_city.title: March of St. Timothy
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Judi Morningstar (White Lake), Oct 2, 1984, named for St. Timothy's Church, Detroit, home of the Detroit Country Dancers' monthly dance for 10+ years.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Grace Waltz
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Attributed to Detroit publisher O. F. 'Cub' Berdan (1880s), named for his daughter.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Ticknor's Quadrille / Lady of the Lake (5)
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Third change of 'Ticknor's Quadrille', recorded by the Henry Ford Orchestra in 1926; now a contra tune popularized by Pete Sutherland.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Old Southern Schottische / 'A Southern Schottische'
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Played in Michigan 'at least since the days of Henry Ford's orchestra'; Henry Ford's Old Fashioned Dance Orchestra recorded 'A Southern Schottische' (Columbia 555-D, Jan 16, 1926).

tunes_named_for_city.title: The Trip to Michigan
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Modern composition by Erica Braverman, written on a Thanksgiving trip to Michigan.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Michigan-I-O
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Lomax recorded Lester Wells singing it in Traverse City (Sept 1938); a 2022 slip jig by Aidan Morales borrows its first part. Michigan, not Detroit.

tunes_named_for_city.title: The Flowers of Michigan (alias of 'Lady Birr')
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Alias only; no Michigan origin documented.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Ypsilanti (alias of 'The Thames' hornpipe)
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Alias; likely named for the Greek general Ypsilantis (as is the Michigan city) rather than the town. Outside MSA.

headline_stats.distinct_traditions_active_note: Approximate: ~13 traditions in layers 1-3 (Irish session; céilí/set dance; Scottish country dance; contra; old-time jam; bluegrass jam; international/Balkan folk dance; old-time and queer square dance; folk-society song swap; community singing; songwriter open stages; gospel quartet and mass choir; lined-out hymnody) plus ~32 heritage traditions rated thriving/active/niche/fading-but-alive (Arab takht, dabke, Chaldean wedding music, Yemeni bara', Polish folk dance, Polish and Slovenian polka, Ukrainian bandura and dance, Croatian tamburica, Serbian kolo, Hungarian, Slovak, Albanian, Greek, Armenian, Maltese, Finnish, Scottish piping, Mexican folklórico, mariachi, conjunto, powwow, Caribbean carnival, West African dance, blues, Hmong, Bangladeshi, Indian classical, Chinese lion dance, taiko/Bon odori, Filipino rondalla).
headline_stats.note: Totals count series inside the six MSA counties with 2024-26 evidence. Excluded from totals: five blues jams on the Detroit Blues Society list (undated aggregator evidence, 21.6/month, low confidence; Detroit's blues jam culture is real but unverified for 2026), Cadieux Cafe feather-bowling league nights (a Belgian folk game, not music), and all Ann Arbor/Washtenaw, Lansing and Windsor events (outside_msa). Modern Western club squares (8 SEMA clubs) were not enumerated as events. Including the blues jams the inside-MSA figure would be about 75/month.

surprises: Washtenaw County (Ann Arbor, ~370,000 people, a separate MSA) runs about as many trad events a month as the entire 4.4-million Detroit MSA; the Detroit Irish Music Association, the local Comhaltas branch, has held its weekly flagship session in Ann Arbor since 2010.

Inside the MSA there is one weekly Irish pub session (Seán O'Callaghan's, Plymouth, since 2023) and one monthly contra (Troy); the busiest trad activity is twice-weekly, Balkan-heavy international folk dance.

Henry Ford never sponsored a fiddle contest (the national 'Ford contest' is a myth built on Ford-dealer contests in 1926), but he kept dance musicians on the Ford Motor Company payroll for 23 years, and his 'American' old-time orchestra featured a Romani cimbalom player, Billy Hallup.
Lovett Hall in Dearborn, the ballroom Ford built for quadrilles in 1937, hosted a contra series from 1981 until The Henry Ford ended it on four days' notice in February 2005; it now hosts weddings.

'Flop-Eared Mule' may descend from the 'Detroit Schottische', published in 1854 by Detroit dancing master Adam Couse and reportedly sold ~100,000 copies (fiddle historian Paul Gifford; others argue a shared ancestor).

Lomax's 1938 Detroit recordings (116 Detroit-tagged LOC items) are mostly Serbian gusle epics, tamburitza and Hungarian songs, plus Delta blues by Calvin Frazier and Sampson Pittman a decade before John Lee Hooker's 'Boogie Chillen''.

Detroit was a Cape Breton fiddling hub: the Five MacDonald Fiddlers, including composer Dan R. MacDonald, formed there, and Detroit police officer Johnny Archie MacDonald ran Saturday 'down east' dances featuring Buddy MacMaster and Winston Fitzgerald. No Cape Breton session survives.
The SE Michigan contra revival began with an impromptu contra at the Detroit Historical Museum's 'Galactic Steam Dulcimer Circus' on Nov 13, 1976.
The newest dance in the city is the Detroit Folk School's monthly Queer Square Dance in Southwest Detroit, which a local paper described as 'dancing on Henry Ford's grave'.
There is no Sacred Harp singing in the MSA, yet The Sacred Harp contains a tune called 'Detroit' (39t), and Ann Arbor's singing meets inside The Ark folk club.
Detroit's public radio station WDET has no local folk show; Detroit's best-known folk DJ, Matt Watroba, broadcasts from WKAR in East Lansing.

The Gospel Music Workshop of America was founded in Detroit in 1967; gospel is the metro's largest singing tradition, and since 2024 ten-plus quartets sing outside the Motown Museum to reclaim the quartet-Motown link.

Seven of roughly 24 music/dance Michigan Heritage Award winners in the metro are blues artists; the Ukrainian Bandurist Chorus, which immigrated as a whole choir of 17 families in 1949, became Detroit's first ensemble NEA Heritage Fellow in 2025.

About 550 students still attend 14 Polish folk-dance schools in metro Detroit (2025 census), while Hamtramck, now majority Arab and South Asian, cheers a parody polka band called 'The Polish Muslims'.
A Dearborn public elementary school has had an Arabic music ensemble since 2002, and the Arab International Festival drew ~250,000 people before anti-Muslim protest costs ended it in 2012.
The Cadieux Cafe claims the only feather-bowling lanes in the US and hosts a Monday blues jam in the same room.
Joni Mitchell wrote 'The Circle Game' in Detroit; the Chess Mate, a real chess club where Bobby Fischer played 51 boards in 1964 before it became a folk room, is now a laundromat.
surprises_all_threads: The 'Detroit' Irish Music Association, the metro's Comhaltas branch, holds its weekly flagship session in Ann Arbor (Grace Ann Arbor North, Thursdays). It has been Ann Arbor-based since 2010, so Detroit proper gets only a monthly Wednesday session plus about two Sunday sessions a month at the Gaelic League.

Inside a 4.4-million-person MSA there is exactly one weekly Irish pub session (Plymouth, Wednesdays at 5 pm, founded 2023) and one regular contra series (Troy, monthly). thesession.org's 'nearby' search within 70 km of Detroit returns only 3 active sessions, and one of them is Ann Arbor.

Washtenaw County (Ann Arbor/Ypsilanti, about 370k people, a separate MSA) runs roughly as many recurring trad dance and music events a month (about 33) as the whole Detroit MSA (about 32): two monthly Grange contras plus a contra party, weekly ECD, a monthly French-Canadian session and Monday Scottish.

Henry Ford hired New England dancing master Benjamin Lovett in 1924 to 'take the shimmy out' of American dancing, co-published the 1926 manual 'Good Morning', and built Lovett Hall's ballroom in 1937. A public contra series ran there from 1981 until The Henry Ford abruptly ended it in Feb 2005 with 4 days' notice. Nothing public continues in the hall today; it hosts weddings.

International folk dance, not Irish or contra, is metro Detroit's busiest participatory trad scene: two nights a week (Royal Oak Mondays; Southfield/Troy Fridays, alternating with the Balkan American Community Center). The Oct 2026 Halloween playlist ran from Romanian horas and Kyrgyz Kara Jorgo to an 'Addams Family Line Dance'.
A single Methodist church in Troy (6363 Livernois) is the suburban trad-dance capital: OCTDS contras, RSCDS Scottish every Thursday, and the annual Starry Night for a Ramble.

Detroit was a Cape Breton outpost: Johnny Archie MacDonald (b. 1893), a Detroit police officer who moved from Judique in 1924, ran 'down east' Saturday-night dances featuring Angus Chisholm, Winston Fitzgerald, Donald MacLellan and Buddy MacMaster (Scotia Sun, 1973). Today no Cape Breton session was found on either side of the river.

The Detroit Old Time Jam (est. 2024) is a potluck in a wheelchair-accessible private house in Northwest Detroit; its website is a tiny GitHub Pages site whose 'last session's songs' links to Slippery-Hill field recordings (Waynesboro, Big Scioty, Katy Hill).

The Paint Creek Folklore Society meets in a 1928 mansion built by a lumber baron and once intended for Dodge heir Danny Dodge, who died on his 1938 honeymoon. It grew out of weekend jams at a 1973 Rochester guitar shop and has held 53 annual Tin Whistle Concerts.

Detroit's Highland Games (St. Andrew's Society, founded 1849) claim to be the longest continuous Highland Games in North America, yet the RSCDS Detroit Branch dates only from 1980, about 15 years after Windsor's group began dancing.

Bluegrass jams happen at a guitar shop in Sterling Heights and a senior center in Westland; the bluegrass association's own jam list has more jams in West Michigan, Lansing and even Ohio than in metro Detroit.
The Oakland County Traditional Dance Society's website has partly been hijacked: its 'dance schedule' and 'sites we like' pages now serve Indonesian casino spam (Oct 2026).

The 4.4-million-person Detroit MSA has no Sacred Harp singing at all. The nearest are 40 miles west in Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti, yet the 1844 tunebook has a tune called 'Detroit' (39t) that singers around the country use.
Ann Arbor's Sacred Harp singing, 'the longest tradition of any active group in the state', meets inside The Ark, a 400-seat folk nightclub, not a church.

Detroit's public radio station has had no local folk show since WDET dropped Matt Watroba's 'Folks Like Us' twice (2004 and Dec 2009). The voice of Detroit folk radio now broadcasts from East Lansing (WKAR), and WDET's only folk-leaning show is the syndicated Acoustic Café, produced in Ann Arbor and added the same week the local roots shows were cut.

The metro's busiest folk room is a ~70-seat former Baptist church theatre in Livonia. Trinity House ran 35 events in October 2026, and its $5 open stage is so crowded that only the first 20 sign-ups are guaranteed two songs.
MAMA's Coffeehouse, now in its fourth decade at a Unitarian church, still takes no advance sales: cash or check at the door only.

The Gospel Music Workshop of America, the giant of choir gospel (75,000 members and 185 chapters by one encyclopedia count), was founded in Detroit in 1967 and held its first convention at King Solomon Church in 1968.
Since 2024 the Motown Museum has hosted 10+ Detroit gospel quartets on Rocket Plaza in a showcase meant to revive 'the rich history and ties between quartets and Motown artists'.

Gordon Lightfoot's 'musty old hall in Detroit' is the Mariners' Church. Parishioners objected and he changed the word to 'rustic'; the church still holds its bell-ringing memorial service every November.

The 2026 Detroit Folk Festival relaunch was a backyard garden party at a songwriter's house: BYOB, croquet, a bonfire 'under the Harvest Moon', a Dolly Parton tribute, hip-hop poet jessica Care moore and a DJ at midnight.

Detroit's strongest instrument makers are classical violin shops (Psarianos, 1976, started in a Murphy-bed closet; Wilson, 1992). The fiddler's shops (Elderly in Lansing, Companion Banjos and MacArthur-winning violin maker Joseph Curtin near Ann Arbor) are all outside the MSA.
WCHB, which signed on from Inkster in 1956 as the first Black-owned station built from the ground up, still broadcasts gospel 70 years later as 'The Voice of the Church in Detroit'.

A Black Baptist pastor and blues singer (Rev. Robert Jones) and a white folk DJ (Matt Watroba) have performed together for 30+ years. Jones received his 2025 Michigan Heritage Award at intermission of a show at The Ark, and his children surprised him with an a cappella song.

Blues is the single biggest 'folk' category in Detroit's state honors: 7 of the ~24 music/dance Michigan Heritage Awards in the Detroit MSA went to blues artists (Sippie Wallace, Howard Armstrong, Little Sonny, Eddie Burns, Alberta Adams, Johnnie Bassett, Rev. Robert Jones).

One of Detroit's four NEA Heritage Fellows is a fiddler: Howard 'Louie Bluie' Armstrong (1990), a Black string-band violinist who spent WWII in Detroit auto plants and called the violin 'just like a third arm'.

An entire choir immigrated as a unit: in 1949 the Ukrainian Bandurist Chorus's 17 families were sponsored out of German DP camps by Sol Hurok and a Detroit lawyer and settled in Hamtramck; 76 years later it became Detroit's first ensemble NEA Heritage Fellow (2025).
Detroit's Highland Games claim to be the longest continuous in North America (since 1849) - i.e., older than the Civil War.

Metro Detroit still has ~550 children and adults in 14 Polish folk dance schools (end-2025 census), and the oldest (Wieliczka, 1955) is shrinking; it and Tatry blame 'the changing demographics' of Dearborn and Dearborn Heights, now the heart of Arab America.
Hamtramck's favorite Paczki Day band is 'The Polish Muslims', a 45-year-old parody polka-rock band, in a city that now has a Muslim majority and a 'Bangladesh Avenue'.
The Polish Day Parade, a 1930s Belle Isle tradition that defined Hamtramck's Labor Day, left Hamtramck for Warren in 2022.
Macedonians reportedly run most of Hamtramck's 'Polish' bakeries, so many paczki are baked by Macedonian Americans.
Dearborn's Arab International Festival drew ~250,000 people (about three times Dearborn's population) before protests ended it in 2012; the region has had no comparable Arab street festival since.
A Dearborn public elementary school has had its own Arabic music ensemble since 2002, and the National Arab Orchestra runs free after-school Arab classical music classes for Detroit students.

Cadieux Cafe is two heritage traditions in one room: claimed to be the only Belgian feather-bowling lanes in the US (its club won a Michigan Heritage Award in 1999) and home of a Monday open blues jam.
A powwow returned to downtown Detroit's riverfront in October 2025 for the first time in 30+ years, with 200+ dancers on ground where Three Fires peoples gathered before contact.

Detroit's Irish fiddle patriarch Mick Gavin (from Meelick, Co. Clare) started what the MSU program calls the longest-running Irish session in Michigan, and taught GRAMMY-nominated fiddler Jeremy Kittel.
Tejano conjunto took root in Melvindale: bajo sexto player Martin Solis Jr. was the first Michigan-based inductee of Texas's Tejano R.O.O.T.S. Hall of Fame.
In 1967 Detroit's tamburica orchestra premiered a 'Romance for Balalaika and Tambura' with the Detroit Balalaika Orchestra, a Croatian-Russian folk orchestra crossover.
Concert of Colors, Detroit's big free world-music festival, was founded in 1993 partly in response to the 1982 killing of Vincent Chin, by an Arab American community leader (Ismael Ahmed, 1947-2026).

Old-time standard 'Flop-Eared Mule' may descend from the 'Detroit Schottisch' (1854) by Adam Couse, a Detroit dancing master who opened the city's first music store and was a friend of Stephen Foster; it reportedly sold about 100,000 copies (WOTFA disagrees on direct descent).

Henry Ford, remembered as the godfather of 1920s fiddle contests, never sponsored one: the 'national Ford fiddle contest' is a myth traced by Paul Gifford to touring fiddler Uncle Bunt Stephens in 1926. Ford did, however, keep a Music Department on the company payroll for 23 years (1924-47).
The 'dulcimer' in Ford's supposedly nativist, Anglo-American dance orchestra was a Hungarian cimbalom played for 20+ years by Billy Hallup, a Romani musician.

In 1928 Ford's dancing master Benjamin Lovett taught old-fashioned dances at Lincoln School, then Detroit's only Black school, and Black Ontario fiddlers Ed and John Campbell were invited to play with Ford's orchestra, complicating the simple 'Ford segregated fiddling' narrative.
John Lee Hooker's day job in 1943 was at Ford Motor Company, the same company that had spent two decades promoting quadrilles to keep young people away from jazz.

Alan Lomax's 1938 Detroit recordings are mostly Serbian gusle epics, tamburitza and Hungarian songs, and his Detroit blues sides by Calvin Frazier and Sampson Pittman (including 'Welfare Blues' and 'Joe Louis') predate 'Boogie Chillen'' by a decade. The LOC tags 116 items to Detroit (52 audio).

French Detroit was a fiddling town: a resident recalled that from 1778 'a fiddle was in every house' along the ribbon farms to Grosse Pointe, and in 1835 a visitor saw French habitants dancing to a Black fiddler calling 'cross over! all hands around!'.

Detroit was a Cape Breton fiddling outpost: the Five MacDonald Fiddlers, including the great composer Dan R. MacDonald, formed in Detroit after meeting at house parties, and the elder statesman Johnny Archie MacDonald was a Detroit police officer.

Joni Mitchell wrote 'The Circle Game' in Detroit as an answer to Neil Young's 'Sugar Mountain'; Young wrote 'The Old Laughing Lady' on a napkin at 4 a.m. in a White Tower opposite the Chess Mate after thieves disabled his car. The Chess Mate, where Bobby Fischer once played 51 boards at once, is now a laundromat.
The Oakland County contra revival began with an impromptu contra at the Detroit Historical Museum during the 1976 'Galactic Steam Dulcimer Circus'.

In 2024-25 the Detroit Square Dance Society, now part of the Detroit Folk School, was running Queer Square Dances at Vámonos in Southwest Detroit, described by Pride Source as 'dancing on Henry Ford's grave'.

Michigan's governor G. Mennen 'Soapy' Williams called a square dance from the stage of a Chrysler UAW hall at 12101 Mack Ave (c. 1955) during the Lazy Ranch Boys Barn Dance era, while a 1953 Wayne State survey ranked 'hillbillies' tied with criminals as Detroit's most 'undesirable' residents.
The St. Andrew's Society of Detroit Highland Games (since 1849, 177th in 2026) claim to be the longest continuous Highland Games in North America, older than nearly every folk event in the US.
The 17 families of the Ukrainian Bandurist Chorus immigrated together as one ensemble in 1949 and mostly settled in Hamtramck; the chorus became a 2025 NEA National Heritage Fellow.

Wayne County's state fiddle championship (Huron Township Applefest, since 1985) requires a schottische, uses blind judging and awards points for Michigan repertoire, a deliberate attempt to define a 'Michigan style' as dance fiddling.
curiosities: Does a college-town satellite out-dance its core metro elsewhere (Ann Arbor vs Detroit; Boulder vs Denver; Cambridge vs Boston; Berkeley vs SF; Chapel Hill vs Raleigh)?
Is international folk dance stronger than contra in other Rust Belt metros (Cleveland, Pittsburgh, Chicago)?
Why did Boston keep its Cape Breton scene while Detroit's (1920s-70s) vanished?
Do Hillbilly Highway metros (Detroit, Chicago Uptown, Cincinnati, Dayton, Akron) keep denser old-time and bluegrass jam scenes in their old migrant suburbs, or did that music vanish as it did here?
Which 1930s field-recorded ethnic traditions (Detroit's tamburitza and gusle) survive as living practice in each metro, and which metro has the most active tamburica orchestras today?
How many big-metro NPR stations have no local folk show, and does that track with weaker listening scenes?
Can gospel quartet anniversary programs be counted and compared across Detroit, Memphis, Birmingham, Chicago and Houston?
When an ethnic enclave turns over (Hamtramck, Delray), do heritage institutions follow the diaspora to the suburbs or vanish? Compare Pilsen, Slavic Village, Polish Hill.
Did any other industrialist put folk musicians and dance teachers on the payroll as Ford did, and with what legacy?
Where and when did queer and gender-neutral square dances start, and are they drawing younger dancers faster than mainstream contras?
Does any other state's heritage-award roster tilt as far toward blues for its biggest city?
Is the schottische more central to Midwestern contest and dance repertoire than elsewhere (Michigan contest rules require one)?
curiosities_all_threads: Why did Detroit's Irish session scene relocate to the suburbs and Ann Arbor? Detroit proper had weekly sessions in 2005-07 (Baile Corcaigh) and 2013-15 (Gaelic League) but now has none weekly. Is this the same suburb/college-town pull seen in Cleveland or St. Louis?

Does the Washtenaw-outweighs-Detroit pattern (a college-town satellite out-dancing the core metro) also hold for Lansing vs Grand Rapids, Boulder vs Denver, Chapel Hill vs Raleigh, or Bloomington vs Indianapolis?

How many US metros have a historically significant contra venue that was shut to dancers (Lovett Hall, 2005), and did the scene recover elsewhere? Compare Detroit 2005 with other venue losses, such as Boston-area halls.

International folk dance clubs (Balkan-heavy repertoire, recorded music) seem to outlast contra in rust-belt metros. Is IFD stronger relative to contra in Detroit, Cleveland, Pittsburgh and Chicago than on the coasts?

Detroit had a strong Cape Breton migrant fiddle community (1920s-1970s); Boston's survives as a scene but Detroit's apparently does not. What made the difference: auto-industry dispersal to suburbs, the 1980s Canadian return migration, or the absence of a dedicated hall?

What share of each metro's Irish session activity is run by a Comhaltas branch versus pubs or independent nonprofits? Detroit now has two competing or complementary nonprofits, DIMA (CCE, 1970s) and the Irish Music Institute (2022).

Hammered dulcimer plus fiddle is described as 'a staple of dance bands in Michigan'. Is the hammered dulcimer measurably more common in Michigan dance bands (Golden Griffon Stringtet, Ruffwater/Morningstar circle) than in other states' contra bands, and why?
Which metros have a Highland Games older than their Scottish country dance branch by more than a century (Detroit: 1849 vs 1980), and does the length of that gap predict anything?

Old-time music in Detroit appears confined to one house jam (est. 2024), despite large mid-century Appalachian migration to the city (the 'hillbilly highway'). Where did the Appalachian string-band tradition go in Detroit, compared with Cincinnati, Dayton or Chicago's Uptown?

Why does shape-note singing thrive in the college towns around Detroit (Ann Arbor, Ypsilanti, Lansing, Kalamazoo, Grand Rapids) but not in the metro itself? Is this core-versus-college-town split typical of other top-20 metros?
How many top-20-metro NPR stations have no locally produced folk program? WDET's history (cut 2004, restored, cut 2009) against WFUV, WAMU's Bluegrass Country, KUOW, WXPN and others.

Gospel quartet anniversary programs as folk practice: how many happen a year in Detroit versus Memphis, Birmingham, Chicago and Houston? Can church bulletins or DetroitGospel.com be mined for a count?
Are Unitarian and Methodist churches the backbone of suburban folk coffeehouse series nationally (MAMA's at Birmingham Unitarian, Green Wood at Methodist churches)?

In Rust Belt metros, has the folk listening scene moved to the suburbs (Livonia, Plymouth, Bloomfield Hills, Farmington Hills) while the core keeps only bar-based songwriter open mics (Hamtramck) and DIY house festivals?
After the 2021 TikTok shanty boom, which metros got recurring pub shanty sings, and why not Detroit despite Great Lakes maritime history and documented Black Great Lakes sailor songs?
How many top-20 metros have a city-named folk festival, and are they institutional (Philadelphia) or DIY revivals like Detroit's?
Do metros with strong classical violin shops but no folk-instrument store (Detroit) have weaker fiddle scenes than metros with an Elderly-style shop?
Michigan Heritage Awards vs NEA Heritage Fellowships: how well are Detroit's gospel quartet singers represented in state and national folk honors compared with Chicago or Birmingham?
How many metros have a community-sing movement led by one person (Watroba's monthly sings and song-leader training)? Does it survive its founder?
Do other states' folk-heritage award rosters lean as heavily toward blues for their biggest city as Michigan's does for Detroit (compare Illinois/Chicago, Ohio/Cleveland, Tennessee/Memphis)?
Polish folk dance: how do metro Detroit's ~550 students in 14 schools compare per capita with Chicago, Milwaukee, Buffalo and Cleveland Polonia?

When an ethnic enclave turns over (Hamtramck Polish to Yemeni/Bangladeshi; Dearborn to Arab), do heritage institutions follow the diaspora to the suburbs (parade to Warren) or dissolve? Compare Chicago's Pilsen, Cleveland's Slavic Village, Pittsburgh's Polish Hill.
Which US metro has the most active tamburica orchestras today: Detroit (DTO since 1957), Pittsburgh (Duquesne Tamburitzans), Chicago, or Cleveland?
Is the National Arab Orchestra unique in scale among US Arab music ensembles, and do NYC, LA or Houston have anything like Dearborn's school-based Arab music programs?
How many US Highland Games claim to be the 'oldest continuous' (Detroit 1849; San Francisco's Caledonian Club 1866; others), and what are the documented first dates?
Why did downtown Detroit go 30 years without a powwow while other urban Indian centers (Chicago, Minneapolis) kept annual city powwows going?
Belgian feather bowling: is Cadieux truly the only US venue, or do Belgian-American enclaves in Moline IL, Green Bay WI or Mishawaka IN keep lanes?
Did the Appalachian 'Hillbilly Highway' leave a measurable trace in today's bluegrass/old-time jam density in Taylor, Hazel Park and Ypsilanti compared with Cincinnati, Dayton and Columbus?
Why does Latino Detroit (thriving folklorico, mariachi) show no son jarocho fandango or bomba scene when Chicago, Philadelphia and LA have them?

Did any other industrialist besides Ford put a folk-dance band and dance teachers on the company payroll (e.g., Endicott-Johnson, Hershey, Kohler), and did those programs leave living dance traditions the way Ford's helped seed squares nationally?

Detroit, Boston and Toronto all drew Cape Breton migrants in the 1920s-50s. Why did Boston keep a strong Cape Breton scene while Detroit's Five MacDonald Fiddlers era seems to have left no regular Cape Breton session in the metro today?

Lomax's 1938 Detroit sessions documented South Slavic tamburitza and gusle. Which Lomax/WPA-documented ethnic traditions survive as living community practice in each big metro (e.g., tamburitza in Detroit vs. Pittsburgh vs. Chicago)?

Among 'Hillbilly Highway' destinations (Detroit, Chicago, Cincinnati, Dayton, Columbus, Akron), which still have dense old-time/bluegrass jam scenes, and do they cluster in the old migrant suburbs (Hazel Park, Taylor, Ypsilanti) rather than the city core?

Why does a college town just outside the MSA (Ann Arbor's Ark, AACTMAD and Folk Festival) anchor the folk scene of a 4.4-million metro? Compare Boulder/Denver, Cambridge/Boston, Berkeley/SF, Bloomington/Indianapolis.
Queer and gender-neutral square/contra dances: when and where did they start (Detroit 2024 vs. other cities), and are they growing dance attendance among under-35s faster than mainstream contras?

Is the schottische more common in Midwestern contest and dance repertoires than in other regions (Michigan's contest requires one), and is this a legacy of Ford-era and Scandinavian/German dance programs?

Of the 1960s coffeehouses in each metro (Chess Mate, Raven, Living End, Retort here), which survived, and does survival correlate with nonprofit or church sponsorship (The Ark was founded by four churches)?

French colonial fiddling: is any distinct French fiddle repertory still played on the Detroit River (Windsor/Essex County, Monroe, Detroit), as in Old Mines, Missouri or Louisiana, or has it vanished entirely?

How many fiddle tunes are named after each big metro, and does the count track population, age or Celtic diaspora (Detroit has a Cape Breton 'Detroit' jig and the 'Detroit Schottische' but surprisingly few others)?
data_quality_notes:
web_search was heavily rate-limited for all Detroit threads; agents used direct fetches, DuckDuckGo/Brave result pages and organization APIs (Gaelic League WordPress feed, AACTMAD iCal, LOC API). Undercounted: Facebook-only events (gospel quartet anniversaries, church concerts, ethnic dance rehearsals, some pub sessions), house concerts. Blues jams come from an undated Detroit Blues Society list and an aggregator; excluded from totals. Detroit Old Time Jam has no posted 2026 dates (medium). Detroit Folk School Queer Square Dance added by the merger from the school's events page and a search summary (Oct 17, 2026 at Vámonos; cadence assumed monthly, medium confidence). Ukrainian, Hungarian and Serbian rehearsal schedules lack 2024-26 evidence. Michigan State Championship Old-Time Fiddlers Contest: no evidence since 2014. tunearch.org blocked direct access (quoted via search snippets). No source found on Anishinaabe/Wyandot music in early Detroit. Founding-date disagreements: Ann Arbor Folk Festival 1976 (The Ark) vs 1977/78; Concert of Colors 1992 vs 1993; Chess Mate closing 1971 vs 1973; Highland Games 1849 is the Society's founding year (first Games unverified). Michigan Heritage Award counts (43 of 147 in the MSA) are the heritage agent's tally. Spot checks by the merger: Ghost Light is open with a weekly Tuesday songwriter night (corrected a 'closed Aug 2026' note).

Thread notes:
[trad] Coverage: Irish sessions (thesession.org API plus the Gaelic League events API, DIMA, IMI and the miIrish Google Calendar), contra/ECD (OCTDS, AACTMAD Google Calendar, CDSS events API), Scottish (RSCDS Detroit and Windsor, Tartan & Thistle), international folk dance (IFDC Detroit Google Group, fresh Oct 2026), bluegrass (SMBMA jam list Oct 2026), old-time (detroitoldtime.com JSON). Gaps and uncertainties: (1) web_search was heavily rate-limited, so Facebook-only events (pub sessions in Royal Oak, Ferndale, Birmingham, Wyandotte; Windsor Irish sessions; Polish, Hungarian or Ukrainian participatory dance nights) could not be checked; none were confirmed, which does not prove absence. (2) Detroit Old Time Jam: no 2026 dates posted; 2026 status unverified. (3) The OCTDS schedule is partly obscured by its spam-hijacked subpages; start times have shifted from 7:30 pm to about 5:00-5:30 pm and the usual day is the 4th Saturday with exceptions. (4) No morris, sword or rapper team, regular ECD series, dedicated Scandinavian group, klezmer jam or Hungarian tanchaz was found inside the MSA; Ann Arbor has a Scandinavian jam (2nd/4th Mondays, Bruce Sagan) whose recurring entry dates from 2022 with no fresh evidence, so it is excluded from the census. (5) Modern western square dance: 8 SEMA member listings, but club nights and frequencies were not verified, so they are excluded from the census. (6) The 'Detroit Contra Dance' at Central United Methodist (23 E Adams, caller Maeve Devlin, Mar 2 2024) appears to have been a one-off for the congregation and public; no series found. (7) DIMA's founding year and SMBMA's founding year were not published. (8) The Detroit Old Time Jam host address appears in a public calendar but is withheld here as a private residence.
[song] Coverage: Layer 2 (listening rooms, coffeehouses, house concerts, open mics, song circles, folk radio), Layer 3 (Sacred Harp, shanties, Black gospel quartet and choir as community practice, the Mariners' Church ritual), plus instruction and shops. Arab/Chaldean and other heritage singing is left to the heritage thread (only Ismael Ahmed and the Concert of Colors are noted). Gaps: no current folk-specific podcast or label found in the MSA; CBC Windsor folk programming not found; Audra Kubat's Union Street open mic status unknown; the GMWA Detroit chapter's current rehearsal schedule and size not found; the 2026 Motown quartet showcase not verified; a Michigan State Sacred Harp Convention does not appear in current fasola Michigan listings (the closest annual singings are Mid-Michigan in Lansing and Kalamazoo). [song] Gospel quartet and choir activity is large but runs through church bulletins, Facebook and word of mouth, so it is badly undercounted here. Strong coverage: the Ford dance revival (with Gifford's revisionist view of the fiddle-contest myth), the Lomax 1938 Detroit sessions (counts from the loc.gov JSON API: 116 Detroit-tagged items, 52 sound recordings), French-era fiddling (county-history quotes via michiganfiddle.com), the Cape Breton diaspora, the 1960s coffeehouses, the Oakland County contra revival (Paint Creek history PDF), NEA and Michigan Heritage awardees, and 2024-26 developments. Gaps and caveats: (1) tunearch.org blocked direct fetches (403), so its annotations are quoted from search-result snippets; (2) no source found that documents Anishinaabe or Wyandot music specifically in early Detroit, and contemporary powwow history was not researched; (3) Burton Historical Collection holdings not itemized; (4) attendance figures for the Highland Games, Motor City Irish Fest and Ann Arbor Folk Festival not found (Wheatland's is low confidence); (5) the Huron Township fiddle contest has no 2024-26 evidence; (6) the Raven's closing (c.1979-80), the Living End's dates and the Chess Mate's closing (1971 vs 1973) are uncertain; (7) Lovett's arrival in Dearborn is dated 1924 (The Henry Ford) and 1928 (another account); (8) Billy Hallup's origin is given as Cleveland, Braddock PA, or Slovak Romani parents depending on the source; (9) the first Ann Arbor Folk Festival is 1976 per The Ark but 1977 in many sources; (10) the Detroit Country Dance Society's later history and the end of the St. Timothy's dance were not traced; (11) Detroit Polish, Arab, Greek, Mexican and gospel histories are only touched on (heritage threads should cover them).
